name: Fractional CO2 laser (CO2RE, UltraPulse, SmartXide)
lead: Fractional CO2 laser resurfacing uses a 10,600 nm carbon dioxide laser, invented by C. Kumar N. Patel at Bell Labs in 1964 [1], delivered in a grid of tiny pinpoints that vaporize microscopic columns of skin while leaving untreated skin between them. Commercial systems include CO2RE, UltraPulse and SmartXide.

People use it to change how skin looks and feels: shallower acne scars, smoother texture, softer deep wrinkles and sun damage, and flatter burn or surgical scars. The chain is controlled injury, then healing: the laser removes damaged surface tissue and heats the deeper dermis, which prompts fibroblasts to lay down new collagen and elastin, and the skin remodels over the following weeks and months [6]. Published studies include burn-scar cohorts, acne scar studies in Asian patients, meta-analyses and randomized trials combined with other therapies [2][3][4][5][14].

Because the CO2 wavelength produces more heat than erbium lasers, Wikipedia notes a higher risk of hypopigmentation and scarring [6]. The device class has also been studied for vaginal atrophy, outside the appearance focus of this wiki [7][8].

paras: Ablative resurfacing vaporizes tissue to create controlled wounds, and healing replaces the damaged surface with new skin [6]. Early CO2 resurfacing treated the whole surface at once; Wikipedia credits Thomas L. Roberts III with developing the CO2 technique in the 1990s [6]. Fractional delivery treats hundreds to thousands of tiny spots per square inch and spares skin between them, which shortens healing compared with full-surface treatment [6]. Systems such as UltraPulse, CO2RE and SmartXide are brand names for fractional CO2 platforms used in dermatology [5].

The Wikipedia overview lists deep wrinkles, sun damage, age spots, acne and surgical scars, stretch marks and actinic keratosis among indications for resurfacing lasers [6]. A review of CO2 and fractional CO2 lasers in dermatology covers scar remodeling, photoaging and other skin conditions [2]. Studies have also used it around the eyes for wrinkles and lid laxity [15], on cleft-lip and cesarean scars [11][12], and followed by topical agents for melasma [13].

A large prospective before-and-after cohort reported remodeling of hypertrophic burn scars with long-term follow-up [3]. A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis of six articles with 467 patients with depressed acne scars found ultra-pulse fractional CO2 laser scored higher for skin smoothness than comparison methods (standardized mean difference 0.49) [14]. A randomized split-face study combined adipose stem cell exosomes with fractional CO2 laser for acne scars [4], and a randomized trial used fractional CO2 laser to intensify photodynamic therapy of actinic keratoses [9]. More recent randomized trials compare it with fractional erbium laser for scars and test add-on topicals for acne scars and burn-scar pigment [16][17][18]. An 80-person randomized trial paired low-energy ultrapulse CO2 laser with platelet-rich plasma for periorbital rejuvenation [15].

Wikipedia states that CO2 resurfacing produces more heat than erbium lasers and so carries a higher risk of hypopigmentation and scarring; other reported complications include hyperpigmentation, acne and herpes outbreaks, the latter two seen in a study of 961 fractional treatments [6]. Downtime is longer than for non-ablative fractional lasers, with redness, swelling and crusting during healing.

Within appearance-improvement circles it sits among the heavier procedures that dermatologists use for acne scarring and deep lines, in contrast to gentler non-ablative lasers. Users generally weigh the longer healing period and pigment risks against results from a single device class that has a large published literature [2][6].

Controlled and cohort studies exist for scars [3], acne scars [4][14], periorbital rejuvenation [15], and actinic keratosis [9]. Randomized trials have compared fractional CO2 with fractional erbium laser for immature and mature scars and tested latanoprost on hypopigmented burn scars and timolol or insulin on acne scars [16][17][18]. Registered trials include acne scars in Asians (n=12) [10], cesarean-section scars [11], cleft-lip scars (n=120) [12] and melasma with topical agents [13]. Studies on vulvovaginal atrophy include a randomized trial against topical estriol [7] and pilot studies [8], noted here only as related uses of the device category.

card.summary: The heavy-duty fractional laser for scars and deep wrinkles: best-studied, more downtime and risk than gentle lasers.
card.note: Higher risk of pigment loss and scarring than erbium lasers.

quick.overview:
Fractional CO2 lasers vaporize tiny columns of skin to resurface scars, wrinkles and photodamage. They are among the more intensive options in laser resurfacing.

Published support includes cohort studies and randomized trials, mainly for scars.
quick.mechanism: The 10,600 nm beam is absorbed by water in tissue, ablating microscopic channels and triggering collagen remodeling; untreated skin between channels speeds healing.
quick.risks: Reported risks include hypopigmentation, hyperpigmentation, scarring, acne and herpes outbreaks [6]. Recovery is typically longer than for non-ablative lasers.

chain: Ablates microscopic columns of skin in a grid
Smoother texture, shallower scars, softer wrinkles
angle.text: It is a clinic procedure for scars, deep lines and photoaging, performed by dermatologists and plastic surgeons, with several days of visible healing afterwards. Results develop as collagen remodels over months.
